entry.title: Phase 3b: two hypotheses fix the course, not the speed
entry.summary: Phase 3 found a network that beats a tuned IMM tracker after a target turns, but that averages
entry.content:
Phase 3 found a network that beats a tuned IMM tracker after a target turns, but that averages "turned" and "not turned" on targets that hold course. Phase 3b gave the network a way out. It outputs two estimates and the probability that the target has turned, and reports the more probable estimate.

It half worked. On the same validation split:

MeasurePhase 3bPhase 3aIMM trackerLimit
After a turn: median range error10.3%10.5%13.6%below the IMM
After a turn: median course error14.5°14.4°24.1°below the IMM
Held course: course error6.1°11.1°5.0°10°
Held course: speed error1.15 kt1.60 kt0.71 kt1 kt

The speed interval, [1.05, 1.25] kt, lies wholly above the limit. The pre-registered rule therefore stopped phase 3b at validation, and its test split was never scored. Under SRD Annex B, this was the last phase-3 attempt.

Records: results and the validation record.

What was tested​

Only the network's output changed. The data, the frozen IMM reference and the gate were all as in phase 3.

  • The network gives a held-course estimate, a turned estimate, and P(turned).
  • The flag's training. The training label is the truth: has the target's course changed yet?
  • The forecast in the decision record, written before training, was held-course course about 6° and speed about 0.95 kt (0.8–1.2), with a 40% chance of reaching the test split.

What happened​

  • Course: fixed. Held-course course error fell from 11.1° to 6.1°, as forecast. It no longer grows with time.
  • After a turn: unchanged. The network still beats the IMM by about a quarter on range and 40% on course.
  • Speed: not fixed. Speed fell from 1.60 to 1.15 kt, inside the forecast band but above the limit.

The flag explains the speed failure:

  • It detects real turns well. The median delay is 70 s, and it misses 0.5%.
  • It also false-alarms. On 29–31% of held-course rows five and ten minutes after the zig, it calls "turned". In this data, those minutes are when targets usually start to turn.
  • A false alarm is costly. The turned estimate is biased slow, so each one costs about 1.8 kt.
  • Even without false alarms, speed sits at the limit. Where the network says "held", its speed error is 1.00 kt, so a perfect flag would leave it there too. The IMM manages 0.71 kt and batch least squares 0.31 kt.

Reading it critically​

  • Switching moves the failure rather than removing it. An averaged output blurs every estimate a little. A switched output is sharp, but sometimes sharply wrong: held-course course P90 rose from 34° to 51°.
  • No threshold tuning. A stricter threshold than 0.5 would cut false alarms but slow detection. Choosing it on this split would make validation a training signal, so it was not done.
  • Two changes at once. The output form and its supervision changed together, as declared, so this result cannot separate them.
  • The finding is consistent. Two different network designs beat a tuned tracker after a turn, and both give back accuracy on targets that hold course. Neither dominates the tracker, and dominating it is what gate G4 asks.

What next​

SRD Annex B §B.5's second branch applies, as it did for phase 3:

  1. publish the negative result, which this post does;
  2. the owner then decides separately whether an end-to-end learned tracker is a new project.

Real or recorded data stay deferred either way.

entry.title: Phase 4 plan: two learned trackers, judged on manoeuvring targets
entry.summary: Phases 3 and 3b ended the same way. A network beats a tuned IMM tracker after a target turns,
entry.content:
Phases 3 and 3b ended the same way. A network beats a tuned IMM tracker after a target turns, but gives that back on targets that hold course. SRD Annex B left the next step to the owner, who chose the separate project it names: an end-to-end learned tracker.

SRD Annex C fixes the design before any code is written.

Two trackers, one gate​

  • A learned-gain filter (KalmanNet-style). The bearing and motion physics stay explicit, and a recurrent network learns the gain: how fast to adapt when the bearings stop fitting a straight track. The hope is filter accuracy on straight legs and network agility after a manoeuvre.
  • A pure recurrent tracker. The LSTM family we already have, outputting position, velocity and its own uncertainty at every step. It is the simpler bet, carrying the known weakness: on straight-leg speed it has stayed at about 3 × classical for six iterations.

Both are trained from scratch on the same data and judged on the same rows.

A harder problem​

Generator 0.5.0 gives the target 0–3 course changes and, in 30% of scenarios, a speed change. Manoeuvres become the norm, which is where a constant-velocity model should struggle most. The IMM and EKF are re-tuned for it, and the better one is frozen before training.

Gate G5​

A tracker passes if:

  • it is better overall: its median range and course error, over rows at 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes after the zig, is below the reference's;
  • and it does not lose much once things settle: on rows more than 5 minutes after the last manoeuvre, it is within 1.1 × the reference on range, course and speed.

The second condition stops phase 3's trade, winning after turns by losing on straight legs, from counting as a pass.

The statistics are stricter than before:

  • The bootstrap resamples whole scenarios, because one scenario contributes several rows.
  • Each tracker's intervals are 97.5%, because two trackers get a shot at the gate.

Reading it critically​

  • What follows a failure is not fixed in advance. If G5 fails, the owner decides what follows then. That is weaker than Annex B, where both branches were set before the result. The write-up will say so.
  • The speed bar is demanding. The settled-speed check asks the trackers to come within 10% of a reference that is already about 2 × least squares on straight-leg speed.
  • The learned-gain filter is a risk. Backpropagation through about 300 filter steps may be slow or unstable in tfjs. Its cost is measured before the decision record commits to it.

entry.title: Phase 3: better than the tracker after a turn, worse when there is none
entry.summary: Phase 3 asked the question the earlier gates could not: does a learned estimator have an edge
entry.content:
Phase 3 asked the question the earlier gates could not: does a learned estimator have an edge where the classical model breaks, when the target turns?

After a turn, yes. Five minutes after the turn ends, on the validation split:

MeasureNetworkTuned IMM trackerRatio
Median range error10.5%13.6%0.77
Median course error14.4°24.1°0.60
Gross errors5.7 points fewer

The IMM was the better of two tracking filters tuned on the same data.

On targets that never turn, no. Its course error is 11.1° and its speed error 1.60 kt, both past G2's limits (10°, 1 kt). The pre-registered rule therefore stopped the phase at validation. The test split was never scored.

Records: results and the validation record.

What was tested​

  • The data. The target makes one course change of 30–120° in 80% of scenarios (generator 0.4.0).
  • The reference. We tuned two tracking filters on validation, a single Cartesian EKF and an IMM (constant velocity plus coordinated turn). We froze the better one: the IMM.
  • The network. It is the iteration-4 LSTM design, unchanged, trained from scratch on the new data. Its decision record was committed before training. It forecast about a 30% chance of a pass, with range the likely failure.

What happened​

  • After a turn. The network beats the tracker on range, course, speed and gross errors. Its lead holds whether or not ownship manoeuvres after the turn. The network has learned something the tracker's model does not hold, for example that the target's speed is unchanged through a turn.
  • On held course. It regresses. It reports speeds 1.2 kt too low on median, and its course error rises to 11° five minutes after the zig, which in this data is exactly when targets usually turn.

A network trained to minimise squared error reports an average when it cannot tell whether a turn has started. An averaged velocity is shorter, and its direction is hedged. This is the dilemma every tracking filter faces, between following a turn quickly and staying steady on a straight leg, now inside the network.

Reading it critically​

  • The forecast was wrong in an informative way. We expected range to be the obstacle. Range and course both cleared easily; the held-course control failed instead.
  • The control is strict but fair. It asks the network not to regress below G2's absolute bar on the 20% of targets that hold course. A tracker that is tuned for turns pays a similar price: the IMM is 5.0° and 0.71 kt on those rows, against batch least squares' 1.2° and 0.31 kt.
  • One validation look. This is not a test-split result, and the test split remains unseen. The margins on the failing checks are wide: both intervals lie wholly beyond the limits.

What next​

SRD Annex B §B.5 fixed this branch in advance:

  1. publish the result;
  2. then decide separately whether a different design is a new project.

The new design could be an end-to-end tracker, a network that outputs "turned or not" rather than an average, or a hybrid that uses the network only after a detected turn. That decision is the owner's.

entry.title: Iteration 5: a hybrid passes G3; the network adds robustness, not accuracy
entry.summary: G2 left the models usable but about 3 × worse than the classical least-squares solver. G3
entry.content:
G2 left the models usable but about 3 × worse than the classical least-squares solver. G3 asks for parity: within 1.2 × classical on every metric, and a lower gross-error rate.

Iteration 5 trained nothing. It combined the two estimators: classical's estimate, except where classical fails or the network disagrees by more than 50% on range, where the network's is used.

G3 passes for that hybrid on a fresh test set of 20,000 scenarios (seed 207):

  • Parity. Every median and 90th percentile of range, course and speed is within 0.97–1.02 × classical.
  • Gross errors. Five minutes after the zig they fall from 1.19% to 0.57% (−0.62 pp [−0.82, −0.42]).
  • Validation agreed. It forecast 1.25% → 0.55% on seed 205.

Records: experiments/20261028-i5-g3/. Figures: iteration-5 results.

How we got here​

The owner first chose a model lever for G3: a per-leg steady-track fit as an extra input (Annex A B.2.3). Three pieces of research reshaped the plan before anything was trained:

  1. The per-leg fit doesn't help where it matters. On a long first leg it measures the range-rate ratio well, about 28% error. At the gate points the current leg is only about four minutes old, and the same quantity is pure noise: 37–64 /h of error against a true value near 1 /h. Classical does better because it fits all the legs together.
  2. Starting the solver from the network changes nothing. It gave classical's answer in 99.9% of rows. Classical's gross errors are not bad starting points. They are cases where the least-squares optimum itself is far from the truth: near-unobservable geometry, where any start converges to the same wrong answer. In 91% of those rows the network was still within 50% of the true range.
  3. So the hybrid has to sometimes overrule least squares. The disagreement switch does, without a tuned parameter. Its 50% threshold is the gross-error bound itself.

Reading it critically​

  • It is a hybrid result. The network alone is still 0.956 kt on speed against classical's 0.307 kt. Nothing here says a network matches classical.
  • No accuracy gain. The hybrid's medians are about 1% worse than classical's on course and speed: measurable, and immaterial against 1.2. What it adds is fewer gross errors: the 1.4% of rows where it switches.
  • The switch aims at the metric that is gated. The threshold equals the gross-error definition. That was fixed in the decision record before seed 207 existed, but it means the lower gross rate is partly by design.
  • It costs something at short range. At zig + 300 s the switch fixes 82 classical gross errors and causes 21. Those 21 are mostly under 4 km, where classical is sharp and the network's relative range error is large.
  • The gain is early only. Ten minutes after the zig the gross rates are 0.17% against 0.14%: no evidence of a difference. The "lower gross-error rate" is shown at the pre-registered five-minute point only.
  • It grows with noise. At σ = 2° gross errors fall from 4.63% to 1.80%. That is the case SRD §5 calls interesting for ML over classical methods.
  • Still simulation. The target holds course and speed (SRD §3), and the data are mock.

What next​

All four gates are passed: G0, G1, G2, and G3 for the hybrid. The proof of concept has its answer.

  • The network alone extracts usable range, course and speed, but is about 3 × worse than classical.
  • As a fallback it makes least squares more robust in near-unobservable geometry, without costing accuracy.

SRD §5 says G3 defines the bar for the next phase. Natural next steps are target manoeuvres (where classical's constant-velocity model breaks) and an EKF reference. Both are the owner's choice.

entry.title: Iteration 4: velocity outputs pass G2, still 3 × classical
entry.summary: Iteration 4 changed the models, not the problem. It kept iteration 3's three-leg engagements, made
entry.content:
Iteration 4 changed the models, not the problem. It kept iteration 3's three-leg engagements, made the models output a velocity (vx, vy) instead of a course and a speed, and added the derived features (bearing rate, its validity flag, the bearing-line intercept).

G2 passes. The seed-205 test split was inconclusive at 0.981 kt [0.940, 1.031]. The rules allow one re-score on a larger fresh-seed test set, and on seed 206, with 100,000 scenarios and the same frozen models, every check passes.

  • Speed passes. The instantaneous LSTM reaches 0.939 kt [0.926, 0.951] at zig + 600 s on the σ = 1° slice, against 1 kt. The BiLSTM reaches 0.740 kt.
  • Range and course pass easily: 7.3% and 4.7° for the LSTM, 5.3% and 3.1° for the BiLSTM.
  • Better than iteration 3 on the same rows. Range, course and speed are 16–27% better.
  • Still about 3 × classical. Classical reaches 0.32 kt on the same rows. The LSTM is 2.1 × classical on range, 3.5 × on course and 2.9 × on speed.

Records: experiments/20261025-i4-g2-rescore/ and experiments/20261024-i4-g2/. Figures: iteration-4 results.

What changed​

Iteration 3 stopped at 1.10 kt. Its LSTM shrank speed estimates towards the middle of the range: slow targets were overestimated and fast ones underestimated, while classical was unbiased.

  • Velocity components. They give one smooth target for course and speed, with no wrap-around and no out-of-range values. Course and speed are derived from the vector.

  • Not enough on its own. Research R1 showed that removing the bias alone would only reach about 1.01 kt.

  • Derived features. The owner therefore added them, to target the remaining scatter.

  • Models. The iteration-3 configuration (two stacked 128-unit recurrent layers), from scratch on seed 205.

  • Outputs. Log range plus vx and vy divided by the top of the target speed range. The loss weights each component 4×.

  • Pre-registered. The decision record, forecast and validation rule were committed before training. Validation gave 0.94 kt [0.91, 0.98] and carried the pair to test.

Seed-206 test split (σ = 1°)​

EstimatorRange, zig+300 sCourse, zig+300 sSpeed, zig+600 s
G2 threshold< 20%< 10°< 1 kt
lstm-instantaneous7.26%4.70°0.939 kt [0.926, 0.951]
bilstm-time-late5.30%3.13°0.740 kt
iteration-3 models (reported)8.7% / 7.2%6.24° / 4.31°1.12 / 1.00 kt
classical3.40%1.36°0.319 kt
naive39.9%89.8°4.23 kt

n = 49,574 at zig + 300 s and 32,266 at zig + 600 s.

Reading it critically​

  • A narrow pass. 52.6% of the LSTM's speed estimates are within 1 kt, and the P90 is 2.9 kt (classical 1.9 kt). The interval's upper bound is well below the threshold, so the pass is not in statistical doubt. The margin itself is small.
  • The bias is still there. The LSTM's median signed speed error is −0.33 kt, and −1.5 kt for 18–20 kt targets: fast targets are called slow. The re-score's forecast predicted this. Removing the bias would leave 0.86 kt; most of the error is scatter.
  • Short range is hardest. Under 2 km the LSTM is 0.97 kt against 0.72–0.78 kt at 2–8 km, and about 20 × classical. Near closest approach the bearing rate changes fast, and the 3-minute trailing rate lags it.
  • It took two looks. Seed 205 was inconclusive and seed 206 passed. The rule allowed exactly this. Allowing two looks roughly doubles the false-pass rate at a true median of exactly 1 kt, from about 1.8% to about 3.7%. The two points differ by 0.04 kt, about 1.8 standard errors. Most of the difference is chance: seed 205's validation split also gave 0.94.
  • Two levers at once. The record cannot say whether velocity outputs or derived features moved speed.
  • The re-score needed four attempts. Cloud containers were reclaimed mid-run three times, on a run of about 4.5–5.3 hours against containers that live about 4–4.6 hours. The scoring is deterministic and every input is bound by digest. Every attempt produced byte-identical files, and the result was fixed before anyone saw it. The last attempt reused the verified prediction files (tma-g2 --reuse-predictions).

What next​

G2 is passed: the models give usable range, course and speed on the problem as posed. G3 asks for parity with classical, which is about 3 × better on speed and course. That is a much larger step than any lever so far has given. Under SRD §7, the plan moves to G3, and the owner chooses whether and how to pursue it.

entry.title: Iteration 3: a second zig helps everyone, classical most
entry.summary: Iteration 3 changed the problem, not the models. After the owner's realism check in the viewer,
entry.content:
Iteration 3 changed the problem, not the models. After the owner's realism check in the viewer, ownship now zigs twice, and both turns cross the line of sight. The 2c models were trained from scratch on the new engagements. Speed improved by almost half, but not enough: the iteration stopped at validation under its pre-registered rule, and the test split was not scored.

  • Speed fails the rule. The instantaneous LSTM reaches 1.10 kt [1.06, 1.16] at zig + 600 s on the σ = 1° slice. The rule needed an interval reaching below 1 kt. The forecast, recorded before training, was 1.1–1.3 kt.
  • The BiLSTM gets closest of any model so far: 1.02 kt [0.98, 1.05]. It is reported, not gated.
  • Range and course pass easily: 8.8% and 6.2° for the LSTM, 7.2% and 4.4° for the BiLSTM.
  • Classical gains more. On the same scenarios it reaches 0.34 kt, so the LSTM is now 3.3 × classical on speed, against 2.4 × in iteration 2c.

Record: experiments/20261021-i3a-val/. Figures: iteration-3 results.

What changed​

The owner watched iteration-2c engagements in the viewer and judged that, with both platforms on steady legs, there was too little information. An operator without a steady solution would zig again, traditionally across towards the contact. The seed-203 gate data agreed in part: turns that crossed the line of sight gave the best classical solutions, and an earlier zig mainly shortened the first leg (spec 007 research R1).

  • Generator 0.3.0. A second zig 3–5 minutes after leg 2 starts. Each turn puts the target 30–90° on the other bow, by the shorter turn. The first zig keeps its timing.
  • Models. The 2c configuration (two stacked 128-unit recurrent layers, speed weighted 4× in the loss), from scratch on a fresh dataset, seed 204.
  • Pre-registered rule. The decision record was committed before training. The pair would go to the test split only if the LSTM's speed interval on validation reached below 1 kt.

Seed-204 validation split (σ = 1°)​

EstimatorRange, zig+300 sCourse, zig+300 sSpeed, zig+600 s
G2 threshold< 20%< 10°< 1 kt
lstm-instantaneous8.8%6.19°1.10 kt [1.06, 1.16]
bilstm-time-late7.2%4.36°1.02 kt [0.98, 1.05]
2c models (out of distribution)11.4% / 17.7%6.53° / 7.72°2.01 / 1.93 kt
classical3.4%1.43°0.34 kt
naive40.2%89.7°4.23 kt

Reading it critically​

  • The lever worked on the problem, not on the gap. Every estimator improved. Classical halved its speed error (0.61 → 0.34 kt), as the forecast said it would. The models improved too, but the ratio to classical grew on every measure: 3.3 × on speed, 2.6 × on range and 4.3 × on course. The extra information went mostly to the estimator that already uses it well.
  • The "improvement" against 2c is weak evidence. The 2c models were trained on the two-leg problem; on these engagements they degrade to about 2 kt. Beating them shows that training on the new data helped, nothing more. The rule said so in advance.
  • This is an easier problem. Large turns (median 143°) and longer windows make TMA easier for everyone. A pass here would have been a pass on the three-leg problem, not on iteration 2's.
  • The BiLSTM near-miss costs. It took 35 runner-hours over three dispatches to stop by patience. Its interval straddles the threshold, but it is not the gated model, and the pair moves together.

What next​

Four attempts have now failed on speed, with the gap to classical between 2.4 × and 3.3 ×. Changing the engagements again looks unpromising: it helps classical at least as much. The remaining Annex A levers change the models instead: output parameterisation, derived features, training changes or capacity (B.2.2–B.2.5). The next one is the owner's choice, pre-registered with a fresh seed.

entry.title: The engagement viewer: single cases behind the G2 numbers
entry.summary: The gates judged the models on medians over thousands of scenarios. The new
entry.content:
The gates judged the models on medians over thousands of scenarios. The new engagement viewer shows one scenario at a time: the plan, both platforms' course and speed, the bearings, and each gate's carried models beside the classical solver and the naive baseline. It is the first step of SRD Annex A. Its first use is the owner's realism check of the generator, which comes before any change to the training data.

What it does​

  • Regenerates scenarios in the browser from their seed with the pipeline's own generator. No scenario files ship. A test checks the browser path is byte-identical to Node.
  • Runs the models in the browser with tfjs on the CPU backend. The same encoding and decoding the pipeline uses feed it, and a test finds it within float32 tolerance of tfjs-node.
  • Three modes. Truth shows the engagement. Instantaneous shows the causal LSTM's estimate at a "now" cursor, from the bearings up to then. Time-late shows the bidirectional LSTM's estimate at every sample of the window.
  • Every gate's carried pair: iteration 1 (G1 pass) and iterations 2, 2b and 2c (G2 fail).
  • The URL holds the view, so every link below reopens exactly what is described.

The 2c BiLSTM runs in about 1 s for one scenario in headless Chromium; the LSTM in about 0.5 s. The eight models total 4.5 MB.

How it works: the viewer.

A typical engagement​

Seed 203, scenario 97612, instantaneous, zig + 10 min. The 2c LSTM sits near its own median errors here.

At zig + 10 minRange errorCourse errorSpeed error
2c LSTM11%6°1.6 kt
Classical3%0°0.9 kt
Naive41%51°6.6 kt

Before the zig the model still answers, but range is unobservable from bearings alone. The viewer greys that period out. Here the LSTM's range sits well short of the truth before the zig and reaches it only after the turn.

The same scenario in time-late mode shows something the medians hide. The BiLSTM's estimated positions form a jagged path rather than a straight track. Each sample's estimate comes from its own output row, and nothing ties them to one constant-velocity solution. The classical batch solution is one straight track by construction. In this case the BiLSTM's post-zig median speed error, 3.0 kt, is worse than the instantaneous LSTM's 1.8 kt.

The largest speed error​

Seed 203, scenario 95484, instantaneous, zig + 10 min has the 2c LSTM's largest speed error at zig + 10 min among the σ = 1° scenarios: 10.9 kt.

The geometry is hard, not broken. The target starts 2.5 km away and opens at 17.3 kt on a course within about 10° of the line of sight. The bearing barely moves, so speed along the line of sight is weakly observable. The LSTM answers 6.5 kt, pulled towards typical training speeds. The classical solver struggles too: 13 of its 101 post-zig solutions fail to converge, and its median speed error is 6.5 kt. One case cannot say how often this happens; it shows one way the models fail.

A held-out engagement beyond the training ranges​

Seed 201 held-out, scenario 102983, time-late, zig + 5 min starts at 25.8 km. Training ranges ran from 2 to 20 km. The BiLSTM's range estimate starts near 18 km against a true 25 km: in this case the model does not reach ranges beyond those it was trained on. The classical solver has no such limit.

Post-zig mediansRange errorCourse errorSpeed error
2c BiLSTM31%34°6.3 kt
Classical12%3.5°0.85 kt
Naive55%53°7.7 kt

What comes next​

The owner now runs the realism check in Annex A §A.5: do the tracks, turns, speeds and bearing noise look like real engagements? Its record (§A.7) decides which Part B levers, such as larger or more ownship course changes, are worth pre-registering on fresh seeds from 204 onward. Nothing is trained until then.

These three cases illustrate; they do not measure. Frequencies come from the gate experiments, not from cases picked in a viewer.

entry.title: Iteration 2c: G2 failed on speed; the project stops at G2
entry.summary: Iteration 2c was the last attempt the SRD allows under G2. It combined the two levers that each
entry.content:
Iteration 2c was the last attempt the SRD allows under G2. It combined the two levers that each moved speed on validation, a speed-weighted loss and twice the model capacity, and judged G2 on a third fresh test split. Range and course are the best of the project. Speed is not within reach.

Verdict: G2 failed (agent review panel, round 2, no rejections). Under SRD §7 the project stops at G2: no-go.

  • Range passes for both models: 13.5% [13.0, 13.9] instantaneous and 12.1% [11.7, 12.6] time-late at zig + 300 s on the σ = 1° slice, against 20%.
  • Course passes for both: 7.36° [7.05, 7.70] and 6.12° [5.87, 6.41], against 10°.
  • Speed fails for both: 1.47 kt [1.37, 1.52] and 1.53 kt [1.47, 1.61] at zig + 600 s, against 1 kt. Only 37% and 33% of scenarios are under 1 kt. Classical least squares reaches 0.61 kt on the same scenarios, at the Cramér–Rao bound.

Experiment of record: experiments/20261016-i2d-g2/. Curves and slices: iteration-2c results.

What changed​

Iteration 2b showed that weighting speed 4× in the loss moved speed by 0.3 kt; the capacity scan showed that a two-layer 128-unit LSTM reaches the 96-unit model's plateau in half the epochs. SRD §7 was amended on 2026-10-15, after 2b's validation result and before its test scoring, to allow one further iteration combining the two, then stop (decisions 18–20, spec 005).

  • Model. Two stacked recurrent layers of 128 units (203k parameters for the LSTM, 538k for the BiLSTM, against 41k and 123k before), trained from scratch; the CNN and MLP controls at their sizes.
  • Loss. Speed weighted 4×, as in 2b.
  • Fresh test split. Seed 203, pinned by content digest in the plan; seeds 201 and 202 decided the earlier attempts; all three are now reserved in the plan checker.
  • Cost. The BiLSTM took 27.5 runner-hours over five chained jobs in two runs; the LSTM 12.6 hours. Per-epoch cost rose 1.4× and 2.2× against 2b.

The decision record, with a forecast of 1.4–1.6 kt, was committed four hours before training started. Validation gave 1.42 / 1.52 kt; the test split gave 1.47 / 1.53 kt.

Results on the seed-203 test split (σ = 1°)​

bilstm-time-late (2c)12.1% [11.7, 12.6]6.12° [5.87, 6.41]1.53 kt [1.47, 1.61]
lstm-instantaneous (2b, reported)15.3%8.27°1.78 kt
bilstm-time-late (2b, reported)15.8%9.12°1.77 kt
classical8.8%3.41°0.61 kt
naive37.2%90.5°4.44 kt

n = 4,689 scenarios at zig + 300 s (93% of the slice) and 3,038 at zig + 600 s (60%).

The repeated G1 checks: both models at 0.35–0.39 × naive on range (pass); controls beaten; shuffled labels at 1.027 × naive (pass). The time-late model is, for the first time, better than the instantaneous one on range and course, and worse on speed; its "not worse" check fails at three late points without an interval (the paired intervals contain the slack), the deficit late, largest at σ = 2° and worst near the window end.

The trend, and why it stops here​

Iteration 2b (seed 202)speed weight 4, continued1.77 kt1.77 kt
Iteration 2c (seed 203)2 × 128 units, from scratch, speed weight 41.47 kt1.53 kt

Each step moved the instantaneous model's speed by about 0.3 kt (the time-late model's by 0.6 kt then 0.24 kt), and the 2c-over-2b gain is real: on the same seed-203 rows the paired difference is −0.31 kt [−0.41, −0.23] for the instantaneous model and −0.24 kt [−0.32, −0.15] for the time-late one. But a pass needs the whole interval below 1 kt, a median of about 0.93 kt: a further 37%, more than both steps combined. The panel's statistics reviewer put it this way, and the panel adopted it as the no-go statement:

On the fresh seed-203 test split the instantaneous model's median speed error is 1.47 kt (95% CI 1.37–1.52) and the time-late model's 1.53 kt (1.47–1.61): 12 and 14 standard errors above the 1 kt threshold, with only 37% / 33% of scenarios under 1 kt; the interval would still exclude 1 kt with as few as about 80 scenarios (56 for the time-late model). Range and course pass with wide margins. Each iteration moved speed by about 0.3 kt and the result matched validation and the pre-recorded forecast; reaching the gate would need a further 37%, larger than both steps combined, from a capacity lever the scan already showed flat (at 30 epochs with speed weight 1: 192 units 2.25 kt, 2 × 128 units 2.24 kt) and a loss-weight lever that bought 15%. Classical least squares reaches 0.61 kt on the same rows, at the Cramér–Rao bound: the information is in the data; this family of models does not extract it. Caveats: three different test splits across iterations (split-to-split differences at most 1.4 standard errors), one training seed per model, two levers tried.

What the models did and did not learn​

The panel's geometry and numerics reviewers agree on the shape of the failure.

  • Speed error does not follow the geometry. By true range at zig + 600 s the model's error is 1.2–2.0 kt in every band, where classical's falls from 1.6 kt at 20–40 km to 0.1 kt under 2 km. By bearing rate it is flat at 1.3–1.8 kt against classical's 0.4–0.9, and the ratio to classical is largest, 3.7×, in the best-observed band (above 1°/min). By range the ratio reaches 16× below 3 km. Against the per-scenario Cramér–Rao bound the models' median error-to-bound ratio is 1.30, where classical's is 0.66 and an efficient estimator's 0.67, so about twice an efficient estimator in the median and nine times the bound below 3 km.
  • The gains were uniform shifts. The 2c improvement over 2b is −0.2 to −0.3 kt in every range band and at every time. By true speed it came from the bands away from the population mean (3–9 kt and 15–18 kt); 9–15 kt and 18–20 kt moved by under 0.1 kt. That is eased regression to the mean (slope of prediction on truth 0.65 → 0.71, about 16% less shrinkage); scatter fell by only 5–9% (2.23 → 2.11 kt). The term that has to move is the one that moved least.
  • The floor is scatter. With every speed-dependent bias removed the median error would still be 1.35 kt. A bidirectional model that sees the whole window did no better on speed than the causal one.
  • Outside the training range band there is no speed information. On held-out scenarios starting at 20–30 km the models' speed error is 3.4 kt at zig + 600 s, 0.8 × the naive prior, and classical's 3.6 kt is no better. Five minutes after the zig the models beat classical on all three quantities there, because classical fails to converge on a quarter of those scenarios; ten minutes after, classical leads on range and course.
  • Range and course are a different story. They follow the bearing-line geometry the network reads, and five minutes after the zig the time-late model is ahead of classical beyond 10 km and at σ = 2° (14.0% / 7.3° / 1.86 kt against 17.1% / 7.4° / 2.29 kt). That lead is robustness to non-convergence: classical fails to converge on 10–16% of those scenarios and is scored infinite there, while on the scenarios it does solve its course is the better one. Given ten minutes, classical leads everywhere. That early robustness is the project's positive result, and it is not what G2 asks.

Speed from bearings is second-order information: it lives in how the bearing rate changes as ownship manoeuvres. Classical least squares uses it explicitly; the networks, given raw bearings and ownship states, learn a population prior refined by about two knots of scatter.

What the panel found​

Five reviewers, two rounds. Round 1 returned approve-with-findings from all five with no blocker or major finding; every reviewer reproduced the speed medians independently, the reproducibility reviewer re-gated, re-evaluated and re-predicted byte for byte, and the red team found no path from a pipeline error to the verdict. Round 2 approved with wording minors only; the corrections are in this post. Record: review.md.

Nineteen minor findings were answered or fixed. Two are worth repeating: the output scale for speed (ownship's 15 kt maximum) puts targets above 15 kt beyond the normalised range, where the models shrink most (not saturation: the head is linear and predictions reach 19.9 kt), and this lead was never tried; and the models were trained with one seed each, so seed-to-seed variation in these medians is unmeasured.

What was not tried​

Within the SRD's hyperparameter cap, three leads stayed on the table:

  1. Derived features (bearing rate and the bearing-line intercept), built in iteration 2 and never trained on.
  2. Rescaling the speed target to unit variance, or a dedicated speed head.
  3. A per-leg steady-track fit as an input or an auxiliary target, giving the network the second-order quantity it does not extract.

None of them is a lever the record shows moving speed, and the SRD's budget is spent. A follow-on would need a pre-registered validation result with the whole interval below about 0.9 kt from at least two training seeds before another test split is scored.

Where this leaves the question​

The SRD asked whether a network trained on simulated bearings-only data can produce usable range, course and speed. On range and course, yes, with intervals well inside the thresholds and, early in the track, better robustness to least squares' non-convergence. On speed, no: three iterations reduced the error from 2.1 to 1.5 kt against a 1 kt threshold that classical meets with margin. The gate is failed and the project stops at G2.

entry.title: Iteration 2b: speed-weighted loss, G2 failed again
entry.summary: Iteration 2b asks one question: does weighting speed in the loss get the iteration-2 models to the
entry.content:
Iteration 2b asks one question: does weighting speed in the loss get the iteration-2 models to the G2 speed threshold? It changes nothing else, and judges G2 on a fresh test split.

Verdict: G2 failed (agent review panel, round 2, no rejections).

  • Range passes for both models: 14.6% [14.1, 15.2] instantaneous and 15.8% [15.2, 16.2] time-late at zig + 300 s on the σ = 1° slice, against 20%.
  • Course passes for both: 8.22° [7.88, 8.54] and 8.66° [8.29, 9.03], against 10°. The time-late course failure of iteration 2 is gone.
  • Speed fails for both, by less: 1.77 kt [1.68, 1.83] and 1.77 kt [1.67, 1.86] at zig + 600 s, against 1 kt. The same weights before 2b, scored on the same scenarios, were at 2.02 kt and 2.31 kt. Classical reaches 0.60 kt.

Experiment of record: experiments/20261015-i2c-g2/. Curves and slices: iteration-2b results.

What changed​

The SRD allows one more round after a stalled G2. Iteration 2 left three leads (research R19): derived features, speed in the loss, and the training budget. The user chose the loss (decisions 15–17 in spec 004):

  • Loss weight. The speed term of the loss is weighted 4× (loss_weight_speed: 4). Speed contributed about 15% of the loss before; now it is about 40%.
  • Continued, not restarted. Every model (the two carried ones and the three controls) starts from its committed phase-B weights, to 220 epochs at most with patience 6. Because the loss changed, tma-train re-scores the best epoch under the new loss before it resumes; otherwise the old best, on the old scale, could never be beaten and the old weights would be kept.
  • A fresh test split. The iteration-2 test split (seed 201) decided the first attempt and is never scored again. The gate is judged on the test split of seed 202, generated with the same count and ranges and pinned by content digest in the training plan. Train and validation are unchanged.

Three tooling checks promised at the end of iteration 2 arrived with 2b and were on for this gate: tma-g2 checks the plan's content digests itself, refuses a phase decision that is not a git ancestor of the carried weights, and checks that every estimator was scored on the same rows, not just the same number of them. The evaluation page describes them.

The carried set was fixed before training: the 2b models, unconditionally. Phase B is scored beside them on the fresh split and reported, never gated.

Results on the fresh test split (σ = 1°)​

EstimatorRange, zig+300 sCourse, zig+300 sSpeed, zig+600 s

bilstm-time-late (2b)15.8% [15.2, 16.2]8.66° [8.29, 9.03]1.77 kt [1.67, 1.86]

Phase B's numbers here differ from the iteration-2 verdict (2.09 / 2.38 kt) because this is a different split; the intervals overlap.

The repeated G1 checks​

instantaneous / naive < 0.5pass: 0.418 [0.405, 0.432]

The time-late model's knife-edge G1 fail from iteration 2 (0.514) is now a clear pass. Its deficit since G1 was a training deficit, not an architectural one: given the same budget it matches the instantaneous model on every check. The "not worse" check has no interval; the two exceedances (ratios 1.055 and 1.056 against 1.05) have paired intervals that contain 1.05, so this fail is not distinguishable from a pass. What is real is the G1 caveat persisting: the time-late model is slightly worse than the instantaneous one at 17 of 19 points, not better.

What the speed weight did, and did not do​

  • Speed moved by 12–23% (2.02 → 1.77 kt; 2.31 → 1.77 kt), and range and course improved with it. Nothing got worse.
  • It is still 1.8 kt against 1 kt, with the whole interval above 1.67 kt. The models are about three times classical, which is at the Cramér–Rao bound on these bearings: the panel recomputed the per-scenario bound on this split (median 1.05 kt for the bearings to zig + 600 s) and classical's error is 0.62 of it at the median, where an efficient estimator gives 0.67.
  • The gain is less scatter as much as less shrinkage. The slope of predicted on true speed rose from 0.58 to 0.65 and the residual spread fell from 2.38 to 2.21 kt; correcting the shrinkage alone would not help (it would give 2.3 kt). Target speeds above ownship's 15 kt map to normalised targets above 1, where the shrinkage is worst; the output scaling was not changed.
  • The gap is where classical is near-perfect. By true range at zig + 600 s (all noise):
True rangeInstantaneousTime-lateClassical
2–5 km (n 731)1.44 kt1.43 kt0.17 kt
5–10 km (n 2,219)1.55 kt1.53 kt0.57 kt
10–20 km (n 2,568)2.12 kt2.01 kt1.51 kt
20–30 km (n 420)2.98 kt3.08 kt3.54 kt

Classical's 0.60 kt median is carried by the short ranges, where a few hundred metres of range error fixes speed to a fraction of a knot. The models are 1.4–1.5 kt there, flat across bands they resolve well, and only beyond 20 km do they beat classical on speed.

  • The range advantage beyond 10 km is narrower than iteration 2 suggested. At zig + 300 s the models are ahead at 10–20 km (14.2% against 18.6%, all noise) and at 20–30 km (24.1% against 27.4%), but the gap is carried by classical's non-converged tail (117 of 1,806 scenarios at 10–20 km on the σ = 1° slice, scored as infinite error). On converged scenarios alone the two are level, and at zig + 600 s classical is better in every band.

What the panel found​

Five reviewers again: TMA geometry, estimation and numerics, evaluation statistics, reproducibility, and red team. All five returned approve-with-findings in round 1, and none rejected. Every one of them reproduced the speed medians independently, and none found a path from a pipeline error to the verdict.

One latent major, fixed. When a continuation changes the loss, tma-train re-scores the best weights under the new loss before it resumes. It used that value in memory but never wrote it to the manifest, so a chained job (resuming with its optimizer state) compared new-loss epochs against the old-loss number. Had a continuation's first job ended before any epoch beat the re-scored value, later jobs would have kept the old weights silently. It did not happen in this run (the reviewer checked every job boundary in the CI logs), but it could have. The manifest now records the value a later epoch must beat and the source of a continuation, a chained-job test covers the case, and tma-train --check verifies that a finished continuation's kept weights are explained by its record.

What else the panel established:

  • The fresh split is fresh: per-scenario seeds derive from the dataset seed and index, a seed-201 and seed-202 collision would need an index difference of 10¹⁸, and no test scenario shares a seed or parameter set with any of the 100,000 seed-201 scenarios.
  • The fail margin is 16–20 standard errors. Only 30% of scenarios have a speed error under 1 kt; for the interval merely to touch the threshold the test set would have to be about 28 scenarios.
  • The re-scoring worked as specified: the reviewers recomputed the re-scored losses to five decimals and confirmed each model's best epoch was chosen under the new loss. The shuffled control's weights are unchanged from phase B because no epoch beat its re-scored loss, which is the right outcome for a control.
  • Classical's non-converged scenarios (1.4%) are scored as infinite error and included; its 0.60 kt is not flattered.

Nineteen minor findings were answered or fixed in two rounds, mostly record-keeping: the manifests of the committed 2b models do not say they are continuations (the facts are in the review), gate-deciding seeds are now reserved in the plan checker, and the write-up wording above follows the geometry reviewer's corrections.

Record: review.md.

Next​

SRD §7 was amended on 2026-10-15 to allow one further round, iteration 2c, and then stop. The capacity scan (research R20) showed that a two-layer 128-unit LSTM reaches the 96-unit model's plateau in half the epochs. Iteration 2c trains that model from scratch with the speed weight, on yet another fresh test split (seed 203). The decision record, with the forecast (1.4–1.6 kt) and the stopping rule, is committed before training: experiments/20261015-i2d-decision/.

entry.title: Iteration 2: G2 failed on speed
entry.summary: Iteration 2 asks whether the iteration-1 models give a useful estimate on realistic data: noisy
entry.content:
Iteration 2 asks whether the iteration-1 models give a useful estimate on realistic data: noisy bearings, dropouts and a rate-limited ownship turn.

Verdict: G2 failed (agent review panel, round 2, no rejections).

  • Range passes for both models. Median range error at zig + 300 s on the σ = 1° slice is 16.5% [16.1, 17.1] instantaneous and 18.5% [17.7, 19.1] time-late, against a 20% threshold.
  • Course passes for the instantaneous model only: 9.46° [9.02, 9.90]. The time-late model fails at 10.57° [10.16, 11.04], against 10°.
  • Speed fails decisively for both: 2.09 kt [2.00, 2.18] and 2.38 kt [2.28, 2.48] at zig + 600 s, against 1 kt. Classical reaches 0.62 kt on the same scenarios.

Experiment of record: experiments/20261014-i2-g2/. Curves and slices: iteration-2 results.

What changed from iteration 1​

  • Noise and dropouts.
    • Bearing noise σ ∈ {1°, 2°}, half the scenarios each.
    • Dropouts drawn per sample, at 0–10% per scenario.
    • G2 is judged on the σ = 1° slice. The σ = 2° slice and the two dropout bands are reported.
  • A rate-limited turn.
    • Ownship's zig is now flown at 0.5–3°/s instead of instantaneously.
    • The zig time is the end of the turn, so "zig + 300 s" means five minutes after ownship is steady on its new leg.
    • This changed the generator (0.2.0), so G0 was re-run and passed again (panel rounds 1–3, 20261013-g0-i2-r2).
  • Provenance.
    • Every dataset header names the generator's commit.
    • Every model records the header of the data it was trained on.
    • tma-train refuses to resume on different features. tma-g2 refuses to score the test split before the phase decision is committed.
  • Confidence intervals.
    • Every gated median carries a seeded bootstrap 95% interval.
    • A check whose interval contains its threshold is inconclusive, not a pass or fail.

Two training phases, one test score​

The test split was protected by a two-phase rule, fixed before training (research R5).

Phase A ran the G1 configurations unchanged: 60 epochs, patience 3, one seed per model. On validation, the instantaneous model passed range (17.4%) and failed course (10.47°) and speed (2.24 kt), so phase A stalled. The decision record was committed before phase B started: decision.md.

Phase B made one change, the training budget. Every model continued from its phase-A weights to 150 epochs with patience 6. This was the user's choice over the pre-registered default (derived features), and the record says what it tests: whether undertraining explains the gap.

Phase B improved range (16.6%) and course (9.56°) on validation, but not speed (2.12 kt). It was carried by the pre-declared rule: its range error was no worse than phase A's by more than phase A's interval half-width.

The test split was then scored once, for phase B, with phase A beside it.

Results on test (σ = 1°)​

The repeated G1 checks​

These are judged on all rows.

The time-late fail sits on a knife-edge. The interval's lower bound is 0.50035, and with other bootstrap seeds it falls between 0.4995 and 0.5006. It does not decide the gate.

Why speed fails​

The panel ruled out the pipeline:

  • Three reviewers re-predicted phase B independently and got exactly 2.09 kt and 2.38 kt.
  • The model's mean speed is right: 11.58 kt predicted against 11.69 kt true.

The errors come from shrinkage towards the mean instead:

  • The slope of predicted against true speed is about 0.57.
  • Slow targets are over-estimated and fast ones under-estimated: errors are 2.6 kt at 0–5 kt and 2.9 kt at 15–20 kt, against 1.5 kt at 10–15 kt.

The information is there. A per-scenario Cramér–Rao bound on the actual bearings gives a median achievable speed error of 0.64 kt, and classical reaches 0.62 kt. The models are about 3.3 times the bound.

Three things point to how the models are trained, not to a ceiling of the approach:

  • Speed gets little weight in the loss. All four loss terms are weighted equally, and speed contributes about 15% of the loss.
  • Training stopped early. In phase B the training loss was still falling (LSTM 0.400 → 0.377 over its last 14 epochs). Validation loss moved by about ±3% from epoch to epoch, more than the per-epoch gain, so patience 6 ended the run.
  • More epochs barely moved speed. The phase-B change improved range and course but not speed.

Where the models do well​

Range bands at zig + 300 s, all noise levels:

Short ranges carry classical's advantage. Beyond 10 km the models match or beat it on range, and fail grossly far less often. The same holds at σ = 2°: the instantaneous model's range error moves only from 16.5% to 18.4%, while classical's doubles from 8.8% to 17.1%.

On held-out geometry, with initial range 20–30 km (outside training, reported only), the models beat classical on every median:

EstimatorRangeCourseSpeed
Models43.8–44.8%about 36°about 3.6 kt
Classical48.8%50.9°9.2 kt

What the panel found​

Five reviewers: TMA geometry, estimation and numerics, evaluation statistics, reproducibility, and red team. All five returned approve-with-findings in round 1, and none rejected.

Two major findings, both resolved:

  • Phase A's predictions overwrote phase B's on disk. tma-g2 wrote both phases' prediction files under the same names. The verdict was unaffected, because it was scored in memory, but re-scoring from disk would have given phase A's numbers. Fixed: the other phase's files are now tagged.
  • The models were stopped by noise, not converged. Accepted. The verdict is stated for this architecture, these inputs and this budget.

A gate-rule fix. The G2 code failed a check whose interval straddled its threshold whenever the point estimate was at or above it. The spec says that case is inconclusive. The code now follows the spec, and a check passes only if its point estimate is also below the threshold.

Re-gating the committed metrics with the new code gave identical checks, and the reproducibility reviewer re-ran the whole gate byte for byte.

Round 2 approved with only minor findings open. Record: review.md.

What G2 cannot tell us​

  • The speed point covers 59% of scenarios. Only windows that run at least ten minutes past the turn are scored at zig + 600 s, so the figure describes longer windows (decision 13). At zig + 300 s, where 93% are scored, speed is still 2.30 kt.
  • Medians hide the range dependence. The range pass is not carried by short ranges, which are the models' weak band. But a single median mixes a 10–20 km band where the models beat classical with a 2–5 km band where they are four times worse.
  • One seed per model (decision 11). The intervals cover test-set sampling, not training-to-training variation.
  • The course pass is narrow. Its interval's upper bound is 9.90° against a 10° threshold.
  • Targets never manoeuvre. G2 says nothing about tracking a target's own zig.
  • Not done: scoring the G1 models on a turn-only set (reported only, not gated). It is deferred to iteration 2b.

Next: iteration 2b​

The SRD allows one more round after a stalled G2 (decision 5). The leads, in research R6, R18 and R19:

  1. Derived features. Bearing rate and the bearing-line intercept, already built (feature_set: derived), give the network quantities classical TMA works from.
  2. Speed in the loss. Weight it per term, or scale its target to unit variance.
  3. Per-leg steady-track fit. Within each ownship leg, fit tan B(t) = (x₀ + vₓt)/(y₀ + v_yt) to the bearings. The fitted shape constrains relative velocity without needing range, and the residual flags a target manoeuvre.
  4. Budget and stopping. A smoothed stopping criterion or a longer run, since training loss was still falling.

Before 2b scores a gate, three tooling fixes are due:

  • tma-g2 checks the plan's content digests itself;
  • the decision commit must be an ancestor of the weights' commit;
  • the same-rows check compares row identity, not just counts.

entry.title: Iteration 1: G1 passed (panel round 3) with a caveat
entry.summary: Iteration 1 asks the question the whole project exists for: given simulated bearings and the
entry.content:
Iteration 1 asks the question the whole project exists for: given simulated bearings and the ownship track, can a small neural network estimate target range better than a guess from the prior?

Verdict: G1 passed (panel round 3) with a caveat. Both model variants beat the naive baseline by more than 2× at the gate point, with the whole 95% interval below 0.5: instantaneous 0.419 [0.407, 0.431], time-late 0.450 [0.438, 0.464] (medians 16.1% and 17.3%; naive 38.4%, classical 4.6%). The shuffled-label model scores at naive. The machine verdict is inconclusive, because the time-late model is measurably worse than the instantaneous one (1.075 [1.046, 1.108] × at zig + 300 s) although it sees more data; the agent review panel passed G1 under a rule fixed before the deciding run (pre-registered rule 1, SRD §5) and recorded that as the caveat. Experiment of record: experiments/20261012-g1-r2/.

It took two attempts. In attempt 1 (experiments/20261011-g1-r2/) the time-late model was cut off by a wall-clock cap after 25 of its 60 epochs and failed (0.551 [0.538, 0.565]). One pre-registered continuation of that model, to early stopping at 50 epochs, gave the pass. Full curves and slices: iteration-1 results.

The question​

G1 (SRD §5) passes if, for both model variants, the median relative range error 5 minutes after the ownship zig is below half of the naive baseline's, on the same test scenarios. The naive baseline predicts the training-set mean range, course and speed, so a model that beats it by 2× has learned something about the geometry, not just the prior.

The two variants answer different questions. The instantaneous model is causal: its estimate at a given time uses only bearings up to that time, as a real-time tracker would. The time-late model sees the whole recorded window, including bearings after the gate point, and so is a post-hoc reconstruction.

Each ratio is judged with a paired bootstrap 95% interval: pass if the whole interval is below 0.5, fail if it is wholly at or above, otherwise inconclusive. Further checks guard the result: a model trained on shuffled labels must score like naive (leakage), each recurrent model must beat a non-recurrent control, and time-late must not be worse than instantaneous. How these combine is on the evaluation page.

What was trained​

Four small models over the same masked 240-row input window (see models), plus one leakage run, trained on GitHub-hosted runners (4 cores, no GPU). Every model had max_epochs 60, patience 3 on validation loss and a 5.5 h wall-clock cap (max_wall_s 19,800; 2 h for the shuffled run). Epochs are counted from 0, so "60 (best 58)" means the 59th epoch gave the kept weights.

Data: 100,000 scenarios (seed 101), σ = 0.5°, no dropouts, initial range 2–20 km log-uniform; 80,000 train, 10,000 validation, 10,000 test, plus 10,000 held-out scenarios at 20–30 km.

The bilstm-time-late row is attempt 1. Under the protocol below it was continued once, from the epoch-23 weights with no wall-clock cap, and stopped early after 50 epochs (best 46); the other four models are unchanged. One configuration per model; nothing was tuned. In attempt 1 the time-late configuration was started twice with identical settings (one job cancelled, one completed).

Every run (FR-009)​

Attempt 1: why the time-late model was undertrained​

All models shared the same budget in time, not in epochs: a 5.5 h wall-clock cap per model, inside GitHub's 6 h job limit. What the panel found in attempt 1 (rounds 1–2)​

Five independent agent reviewers (TMA geometry, estimation and numerics, evaluation statistics, reproducibility, red team) reviewed attempt 1 over two rounds; the full record, with every finding and response, is in experiments/20261011-g1-r2/review.md.

In plain words:

  • The pipeline is sound. Padding does not leak into the bidirectional pass (padded and unpadded windows give identical outputs); predictions line up with their scenarios; the causal models ignore bearings after the time they estimate; the time-late model does use later bearings (cutting them off makes it worse, 21.2% → 27.2%).
  • The instantaneous pass is real. No truth reaches the inputs or the normalisation, naive is not artificially weak, every comparison uses the same 9,784 scenarios, and the shuffled-label model trained down to the "know nothing" level and scores like naive.
  • Reproducible. A reviewer regenerated the data and re-scored the committed weights locally: the verdict file came out byte-identical, naive and classical metrics byte-identical, model metrics within 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ relative.
  • The time-late fail is a budget effect (one reviewer rejected in round 1 until this was recognised). Calling it "ML not extracting the signal" would overstate it. The first result is recorded as: G1 not passed as run; the instantaneous variant met the criterion; the time-late variant failed under a 25-epoch wall-clock budget and is plausibly undertrained; no evidence that the time-late signal is absent.
  • But no rule allowed a re-run. Turning "undertrained" into "try again" needed an explicit amendment, decided after seeing the result and written down before any new training. That is what the user decided (below), and round 2 approved the protocol with all five reviewers at approve-with-findings.

Smaller findings, reported rather than fixed now: pre-zig rows, never scored, carry 64% of the time-late model's training loss; model manifests lack a git commit field (provenance is recorded in the review instead); training budgets should be set in epochs, not wall-clock time, because runner CPUs vary; the shuffled model's median course error (82.9°) is a little below chance (≈ 90°), a weak bearing-as-course prior rather than leakage.

The decision and the continuation protocol​

The user decided on 12 October, after the first G1 result and before any further training, to continue the time-late model once, to the same 60-epoch budget the instantaneous model had. SRD §5 was amended to allow exactly this, and the protocol was fixed in review.md before the run started:

  1. One change only: no wall-clock cap. Training resumes from the committed epoch-23 weights (digest checked) and runs to epoch 60 or early stopping (patience 3). Epoch 24 of the first run is dropped.
  2. Unchanged: data, splits, training seed, architecture, loss, learning rate, batch size. The other four models are reused untouched; the instantaneous model is not retrained.
  3. Optimizer: Adam's state was never saved in attempt 1, so it restarts once, at epoch 24, and epochs 24–26 do not count towards patience. From then on Adam's state is saved with every checkpoint and restored if a job is interrupted, so a resumed run matches an uninterrupted one (tested: identical weights).
  4. Scoring: the verdict of record comes from re-scoring all five committed models with evaluate-g1.yml on main; the test split is not touched until training completes.
  5. Outcomes, fixed in advance: both intervals wholly below 0.5 and shuffled labels at naive → G1 pass, even if time-late-not-worse still fails (the record then says "time-late not shown better than instantaneous"). A ratio fail of the continued model is final: no further continuation, seed or architecture change, and the project stops per SRD §5.
  6. Record: attempt 1 (0.551) stays recorded as a valid attempt. Every job of the continuation is listed with its run id, epochs covered and runner CPU.

G1 passes under pre-registered rule 1 (SRD §5 as amended 2026-10-12). Both ratio intervals lie wholly below 0.5, instantaneous 0.419 [0.407, 0.431] and time-late (continued to 50 epochs) 0.450 [0.438, 0.464], and the shuffled-label model sits at naive. A small network does extract range information from bearings alone, in real time and in reconstruction, though at the gate point it is still about 3.5× (instantaneous) and 3.8× (time-late) worse than the classical solver.

Caveat, recorded with the pass:

  • Time-late not shown better than instantaneous. It is measurably worse: at zig+300s, 0.173 vs 0.161, a ratio of 1.075 [1.046, 1.108]. Its median is higher at 18 of the 20 gated points, by more than 5% (up to 9%) at 14 of them (120–480, 600 and 720–1020 s). It is lower only at zig+60s (0.984 [0.964, 1.006]) and zig+1200s (0.973 [0.864, 1.126], n 516); neither difference is significant.
  • Not explained by undertraining. The continued model trained to early stopping.
  • The BiLSTM under-uses the future. Its error profile is shaped like a causal estimator's. Masking and the backward pass are verified correct, and truncating the future does change outputs, but weakly.
  • One training draw per variant. Training-seed variance is unquantified.

What G1 cannot tell us​

  • The targets move at constant velocity and the ownship zig is instantaneous; nothing here says how the models cope with manoeuvres or gradual turns.
  • σ = 0.5° and no dropouts only; noise and gaps are iteration 2's question (G2).
  • The time-late model's estimate at zig + 300 s uses bearings recorded after that time. It is a post-hoc reconstruction, not a real-time solution.
  • The interval covers test sampling, not training variation: each model was trained once, and weights differ across runner CPU families.
  • The time-late model was trained in three stretches on three CPU families with one optimizer restart; the instantaneous model in one. The protocol equalised the epoch budget, not the training path, and early stopping ended the time-late model at 50 epochs against 60.
  • The shuffled-label test rules out leakage through labels and the training harness; truth hidden in the inputs is ruled out by a separate counterfactual test.

The full list, with mitigations, is in specs/002-iteration-1-signal/g1-limits.md.

Next: iteration 2​

Iteration 2 (spec 003) runs the same models on σ = 1–2° with 10% dropouts, judged at G2: median range error below 20% and course below 10° five minutes after the zig, speed below 1 kt ten minutes after, at σ = 1°. At σ = 0.5° the instantaneous model is at 16.1% and 9.4° (zig + 300 s) and 1.83 kt (zig + 600 s), against classical's 4.6%, 1.9° and 0.31 kt, so speed is furthest off. Leads from this gate:

  • Pre-zig rows carry 64% of the time-late model's training loss but are never scored.
  • Gradient clipping, against spikes like the one at epoch 48.
  • Both models still follow the training prior by range band, and are held to the training prior on the held-out 20–30 km set; G2 is to include a range-extrapolation check.
  • Why the bidirectional model under-uses the future, before time-late is relied on.
  • Engineering: training budgets in epochs rather than wall-clock time; the runner CPU recorded in re-scored manifests; a cross-process bidirectional resume test; a git commit in model manifests.

entry.title: Iteration 0: G0 passes — the pipeline is verified
entry.summary: The first gate asks a narrow question: can we trust the data before training anything on it?
entry.content:
The first gate asks a narrow question: can we trust the data before training anything on it?

Verdict: G0 pass (machine verdict; team review pending). Experiment: experiments/20261011-g0/.

  • 100,000 noise-free scenarios generated (seed 42); the 10,000-scenario test split was scored.
  • The least-squares solver recovered truth on 10,000 / 10,000 scenarios. Worst cases: 2.9×10⁻⁴ relative range, 0.016° course, 0.002 kt speed (tolerances 10⁻³, 0.1°, 0.01 kt). Median range error 1.9×10⁻⁷.
  • The naive baseline reproduced exactly across two independent fits.

Yardsticks for iteration 1​

On the same noise-free test set, the naive baseline's median range error is 40% (P90 139%), its median course error 90° and its gross-error rate 37%. Any model must beat these to pass G1.

On noisy data (σ 0.5–2°, up to 10% dropouts) the classical solver's median range error is about 5%, with P90 ≈ 43% and gross-error rate ≈ 9%. None of those gross errors were optimiser failures: starting from the true state never found a lower cost. The tail comes from the information in the bearings, not from a weak solver.

Caveat​

Passing G0 shows that generator and solver agree. On its own it would not catch an error shared by both; hand-computed geometry tests cover that separately.

Generation plus the G0 run took about 70 seconds on a laptop-class machine.
